title: Hasimuddin v. State of U.P. & 5 Others
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
date_display: 2 September 2020 (common order in two connected writ petitions)
docket: Writ-C No. 12870 of 2020 with Writ-C No. 13037 of 2020 (connected)
disposition: Both writ petitions partly allowed. The petitioner challenged (i) the assessment order dated 24.10.2018 of the Electricity Distribution Division-2, UPPCL, Mugalsarai, Chandauli, and (ii) the appellate orders dated 2.7.2020 of the Commissioner Division, Varanasi, dismissing his appeals (Nos. C201914000000413 and C201914000000414 of 2019) for want of jurisdiction. The assessment had followed an FIR under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (Case Crime No. 395 of 2018), the deposit and encashment of Rs. 8 lakh and Rs. 7 lakh as compounding charges, and a provisional and then a final assessment. The Single Judge held that assessment in such a case is carried out under Section 126 of the Act (Sections 126 and 135 being harmoniously interpreted, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(6)), that the remedy against a Section 126 assessment is a statutory appeal under Section 127, and that the High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final Section 126(3) assessment when a Section 127 appeal is available. As the State, by notification dated 14.7.2006, had conferred appellate power under Section 127 on the Commissioner of the division, and as this Court had earlier (order dated 18.2.2019 in the petitioner's own Writ-C No. 5391 of 2019) held that the petitioner had the Section 127 remedy, the Commissioner was not justified in dismissing the appeals for want of jurisdiction. The impugned appellate orders dated 2.7.2020 were quashed and the appeals restored to be decided expeditiously, preferably within two months; the assessment order itself was left to be tested in those restored appeals.
headnote: An assessment following an FIR for theft under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is nonetheless made under Section 126, appealable under Section 127; and where the State has conferred Section 127 appellate power on the Commissioner of the division, that authority cannot decline the appeal for want of jurisdiction. The petitioner, running a plastic unit on two connections (20 KV and 30 KV), faced an inspection and an FIR under Section 135 (Case Crime No. 395 of 2018); he deposited Rs. 8 lakh and Rs. 7 lakh as compounding charges, and a provisional and then a final assessment were made, followed by a recovery citation. His earlier writ against the recovery (Writ-C No. 5391 of 2019) had been dismissed on 18.2.2019 as he had a Section 127 appeal remedy; he then appealed to the Commissioner Division, Varanasi, who dismissed the appeals for want of jurisdiction. Allowing the writ petitions in part, the Single Judge held, relying on the Division Bench decisions in Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. and Sanjay Singh v. State of U.P. (and, through the latter, on Executive Engineer, SOUTHCO v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill), that even where an FIR under Section 135 is lodged the assessment is carried out under Section 126 — the two provisions being harmoniously interpreted and the Special Court finally determining civil liability under Section 154(6) — and that the statutory remedy against such an assessment is a Section 127 appeal, the High Court normally declining to interfere with a final Section 126(3) assessment under Article 226 where that appeal is available. Since the State's notification dated 14.7.2006 conferred Section 127 appellate power on the Commissioner of the division, and this Court had already held (18.2.2019) that the petitioner had that remedy, the Commissioner was not justified in dismissing the appeals for want of jurisdiction. The appellate orders dated 2.7.2020 were quashed and the appeals restored for expeditious decision, preferably within two months.
facts: The petitioner, Hasimuddin, had established a plastic unit at village Bahadurpur under the Prime Minister's Employment Scheme and had taken two electricity connections — a 20 KV connection (Account No. 0526577687) and a 30 KV connection (Account No. 2569881000) — with a 63 KV transformer installed; his father held a separate agricultural connection for a 5 HP pumping set. On an inspection of the premises, an FIR under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (Case Crime No. 395 of 2018, P.S. Mugalsarai, Chandauli) was lodged. The petitioner deposited two cheques (Rs. 8 lakh and Rs. 7 lakh) as compounding charges, which were encashed by the department on 11.9.2018. A provisional assessment bill was prepared, to which the petitioner objected, and a final assessment bill was then prepared under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. A recovery citation was issued, which the petitioner challenged in Writ-C No. 5391 of 2019; that petition was dismissed on 18.2.2019 on the ground that the petitioner had the statutory remedy of appeal under the Electricity Act. The petitioner then filed appeals (after depositing the requisite amount) before respondent no.2, the Commissioner Division, Varanasi, who dismissed them (orders dated 2.7.2020 in Appeal Nos. C201914000000413 and C201914000000414 of 2019) on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to hear and decide them. By these two connected writ petitions the petitioner challenged both the assessment order dated 24.10.2018 and the appellate orders dated 2.7.2020. The Single Judge (Hon'ble Piyush Agrawal, J.) decided both petitions by a common order dated 2.9.2020.

reusable_constructions.construction: Even where an FIR for theft of electricity under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is lodged, the assessment is carried out under Section 126 of the Act; Sections 126 and 135 are to be interpreted harmoniously to give effect to the object of the Act, and the Special Court trying the offence finally determines the civil liability under Section 154(6).

The statutory remedy against a final assessment under Section 126 is an appeal under Section 127 of the Act; the High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final Section 126(3) assessment where a Section 127 appeal is available.

Where the State Government, by notification (here dated 14.7.2006), has conferred Section 127 appellate power on the Commissioner of the division, that authority has jurisdiction to hear and decide the appeal and cannot dismiss it for want of jurisdiction.

holding_units.clause: 127 (appeal against a Section 126 assessment) r/w State notification dated 14.7.2006
holding_units.topic: The remedy against a Section 126 assessment is a Section 127 appeal; the Commissioner of the division, empowered by the 14.7.2006 notification, has jurisdiction and cannot dismiss the appeal for want of jurisdiction
holding_units.question: Is the remedy against a Section 126 assessment an appeal under Section 127, and did the Commissioner of the division — on whom the State conferred Section 127 appellate power by notification dated 14.7.2006 — have jurisdiction to hear the petitioner's appeal?
holding_units.holding: Yes on both counts. The assessment having been passed under Section 126, an appeal under Section 127 lies before the appellate authority as prescribed, and the State Government by its notification dated 14.7.2006 conferred the power to hear and decide such appeals on the Commissioner of the division. This Court had also earlier held, in the petitioner's own case (order dated 18.2.2019 in Writ-C No. 5391 of 2019), that the petitioner had the Section 127 remedy. The Commissioner was therefore not justified in dismissing the appeals for want of jurisdiction; the appellate orders dated 2.7.2020 were quashed and the appeals restored for expeditious decision.

holding_units.clause: 126 r/w 135 and 154(6) (assessment despite a Section 135 FIR; Article 226 restraint where a Section 127 appeal is available)
holding_units.topic: Even where an FIR under Section 135 (theft) is lodged, assessment is under Section 126 (harmonious interpretation of 126 and 135, civil liability fixed by the Special Court under s.154(6)); the High Court normally declines Article 226 interference with a final s.126(3) assessment where a Section 127 appeal lies
holding_units.question: Where an FIR for theft under Section 135 is lodged, can an assessment be made under Section 126, and should the High Court interfere with the final Section 126(3) assessment under Article 226 when a Section 127 appeal is available?
holding_units.holding: Yes to the Section 126 assessment; no to Article 226 interference. Relying on the Division Bench decisions in Sandeep Kesarwani and Sanjay Singh, even where an FIR under Section 135 of the Act is lodged the assessment has to be carried out under Section 126, Sections 126 and 135 being interpreted harmoniously to give effect to the object of the Act, with the Special Court trying the offence finally determining civil liability under Section 154(6). No ratio of the Apex Court supports the contention that theft under Section 135 precludes a Section 126 assessment. Following Executive Engineer, SOUTHCO v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill, the High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final Section 126(3) assessment where a statutory Section 127 appeal is available.
